variants.title: Publish one index generation
variants.context: Search is a derived view of authoritative data. A safe indexing path reads a durable change log, transforms once and deterministically, writes lexical and vector artifacts under a generation ID, then validates and switches the serving alias instead of mutating an untracked mixture of versions.
variants.prompt: A batch of edited documents must become searchable. Put the indexing steps in order.

items.text: Normalize fields, chunk text, and compute embeddings while recording the transformer and model versions.
Write the lexical and vector artifacts under one generation ID rather than editing the live index.
Read the durable change log with stable document IDs, versions, tenant boundaries, and tombstones.
Check counts, sampled documents, deletion coverage, and retrieval quality, then switch the serving alias.

variants.hint: Which step is the first one that users can see?
variants.explanation: A generation is published only after every required representation is ready and validated, which is what makes a rollback possible without a full reindex.

variants.title: Publish one index generation
variants.context: Search is a derived view of authoritative data. A safe indexing path reads a durable change log, transforms once and deterministically, writes lexical and vector artifacts under a generation ID, then validates and switches the serving alias instead of mutating an untracked mixture of versions.
variants.prompt: A document was deleted at the source and must stop being searchable. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Write the new lexical and vector artifacts under a fresh generation ID.
Rebuild the affected representations deterministically so both index types agree on the removal.
Validate deletion coverage on sampled documents before switching the serving alias.
Read the tombstone from the change log with the document's stable ID and version.

variants.hint: Deleting from one index while the other still answers is the failure to avoid.
variants.explanation: Deletion propagates through the same generation pipeline as any other change, and tombstones are retained long enough for lagging workers and replay jobs to observe them.

variants.title: Publish one index generation
variants.context: Search is a derived view of authoritative data. A safe indexing path reads a durable change log, transforms once and deterministically, writes lexical and vector artifacts under a generation ID, then validates and switches the serving alias instead of mutating an untracked mixture of versions.
variants.prompt: A new embedding model must replace the current one across the corpus. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Validate recall at the chosen candidate depth, then switch the alias to the new generation.
Replay the change log so every document is rebuilt from the same authoritative state.
Recompute embeddings with the new model version recorded beside each document.
Build the shadow lexical and vector artifacts as one complete generation.

variants.hint: Two embedding generations in one index do not share a coordinate system.
variants.explanation: A model swap is an index generation, not an in-place edit, so the corpus is never partly on one representation and partly on another while serving.

variants.title: Degrade without failing open
variants.context: Hybrid retrieval runs its branches concurrently, each with a child deadline, and the fallback ladder is deterministic: reranked order, then fused order, then a healthy single retriever, then an explicit empty or unavailable state. Authorization and deletion checks never fail open when relevance stages are shed.
variants.prompt: Put the fallback ladder in order, from the best available answer to the last resort.

items.text: Return an explicit empty or unavailable state when eligibility cannot be proven.
Return the learned reranker order when all required evidence arrives on time.
Return the fused lexical and semantic order when the reranker misses its child deadline.
Return the healthy single-retriever order when the other retriever is unavailable.

variants.hint: Each rung sheds one more source of evidence; which loss is never acceptable?
variants.explanation: The ladder is deterministic and tested, and the last rung exists because failing open on permissions or deletion state is not graceful degradation.

variants.title: Degrade without failing open
variants.context: Hybrid retrieval runs its branches concurrently, each with a child deadline, and the fallback ladder is deterministic: reranked order, then fused order, then a healthy single retriever, then an explicit empty or unavailable state. Authorization and deletion checks never fail open when relevance stages are shed.
variants.prompt: One query runs the healthy hybrid path. Put the steps in order, ending with the page that is returned.

items.text: Assemble the page and log the source ranks, versions, and stage timings.
Start the lexical and semantic branches concurrently, each applying its fail-closed eligibility filter.
Stop waiting when a child deadline expires and keep whatever valid evidence arrived.
Fuse the source ranks so the two score scales never have to be compared directly.
Rerank the bounded top set with richer query-document features.

variants.hint: Two branches that run at the same time cannot each own the whole budget.
variants.explanation: Concurrent branches with child deadlines make the expensive stages optional, and fusion works on positions so a missing branch degrades the order rather than corrupting it.

variants.title: Degrade without failing open
variants.context: Hybrid retrieval runs its branches concurrently, each with a child deadline, and the fallback ladder is deterministic: reranked order, then fused order, then a healthy single retriever, then an explicit empty or unavailable state. Authorization and deletion checks never fail open when relevance stages are shed.
variants.prompt: The vector index is degraded and the reranker is queueing behind it. Put the request's decisions in order.

items.text: The reranker budget is already spent, so the fused order becomes the answer.
The vector branch misses its child deadline and contributes nothing to fusion.
Fusion proceeds over the lexical ranks that did arrive on time.
The response records the fallback reason so the incident can be attributed to a stage.

variants.hint: Ask what the next stage is allowed to do with evidence that never arrived.
variants.explanation: Shedding stages in a fixed order keeps a degraded answer explainable, and the recorded fallback reason is what separates a retrieval incident from a ranking one.

variants.title: Budget the retrieval stage
variants.context: Retrieval capacity is budgeted before it is bought. Serving copies are peak queries per second times burst headroom divided by measured queries per second per copy, rounded up. Index memory counts vector bytes, graph bytes, and metadata per document. The end-to-end target is split into child deadlines for each stage.
variants.prompt: A commerce search serves 12,000 peak queries per second and plans with a burst headroom factor of 1.3. Each serving copy handles a measured 250 queries per second. How many serving copies does the plan require?
variants.hint: Peak is not the number the plan is sized against.
variants.explanation: 12,000 times 1.3 is 15,600 queries per second; divided by 250 per copy that is 62.4, and the plan rounds up to 63.

mistakes.feedback: 48 divides raw peak by 250 and leaves no burst headroom at all.
62 truncates 62.4 instead of rounding up, so the last slice of burst traffic has no copy to run on.

variants.title: Budget the retrieval stage
variants.context: Retrieval capacity is budgeted before it is bought. Serving copies are peak queries per second times burst headroom divided by measured queries per second per copy, rounded up. Index memory counts vector bytes, graph bytes, and metadata per document. The end-to-end target is split into child deadlines for each stage.
variants.prompt: A support knowledge base holds 8 million passages with 768-dimensional int8 vectors at 1 byte per dimension, plus 112 graph bytes and 160 metadata bytes per document. How much memory does the index hold before overhead factors?
variants.hint: Work out the bytes for one document before you touch the corpus size.
variants.explanation: Each document needs 768 plus 112 plus 160, which is 1,040 bytes; 8 million documents at 1,040 bytes is 8.32 GB.

mistakes.feedback: 6.14 GB counts only the vectors and drops the graph and metadata bytes that ship with them.
26.75 GB uses 4 bytes per dimension, which is the float32 reference rather than the stated int8 profile.

variants.title: Budget the retrieval stage
variants.context: Retrieval capacity is budgeted before it is bought. Serving copies are peak queries per second times burst headroom divided by measured queries per second per copy, rounded up. Index memory counts vector bytes, graph bytes, and metadata per document. The end-to-end target is split into child deadlines for each stage.
variants.prompt: A query has a 200 ms end-to-end target. Understanding takes 15 ms, the lexical and semantic branches run concurrently under a 60 ms child deadline, feature access takes 25 ms, and assembly plus network take 30 ms. What child deadline is left for the reranker?
variants.hint: Branches that run at the same time are charged once.
variants.explanation: 200 minus 15 minus 60 minus 25 minus 30 leaves 70 ms for the reranker, because the two retrieval branches share one 60 ms window.

mistakes.feedback: 10 ms charges the lexical and semantic branches 60 ms each, but they run concurrently.
100 ms forgets assembly and network time, which are inside the user-facing target too.

variants.title: Make the trade-off explicit
variants.context: Search designs trade recall, latency, eligibility, freshness, and cache reuse against each other. The trade-off is only safe when the constraint that may never be bypassed stays outside the negotiation.
variants.prompt: For one tenant the eligible set is a tiny slice of the corpus, and applying the filter inside the vector search collapses recall. What is the defensible design?
options: Post-filter at display time only, since that is where users see the results.
Pre-filter as before and accept the recall loss for that tenant.
Retrieve deeper, post-filter, and keep a fail-closed authorization check on the path.
optionFeedback: A display-time filter leaves earlier paths able to return documents the caller may not see.
Accepting the loss quietly turns a tunable trade-off into a permanent quality gap for one tenant.
Correct: post-filtering costs depth, and the authorization check stays on every path that can return a document.
variants.hint: Ask which constraint is allowed to be traded and which is not.
variants.explanation: Pre-filter and post-filter are both legitimate, but post-filtering may never be the only authorization check, and it usually needs deeper retrieval to pay for itself.

variants.title: Make the trade-off explicit
variants.context: Search designs trade recall, latency, eligibility, freshness, and cache reuse against each other. The trade-off is only safe when the constraint that may never be bypassed stays outside the negotiation.
variants.prompt: Personalized reranking features raise NDCG on judged traffic, but cache reuse drops sharply and more personal data enters the path. What should ship?
options: Ship it with a non-personalized fallback and measured cost and privacy limits.
Ship personalization everywhere, since ordered relevance improved on judged traffic.
Disable result caching entirely so the personalized path is always consistent.
optionFeedback: Correct: personalization is kept alongside a non-personalized fallback, with its cost and privacy effects stated.
A relevance gain does not pay the infrastructure cost or the privacy obligation it created.
Removing caching converts a ranking change into a capacity problem for every query, personalized or not.
variants.hint: What serves the query when the personal features are unavailable?
variants.explanation: Personalization trades cache reuse and privacy obligations for ordering quality, so it ships with a preserved fallback and explicit limits rather than as a pure win.

variants.title: Make the trade-off explicit
variants.context: Search designs trade recall, latency, eligibility, freshness, and cache reuse against each other. The trade-off is only safe when the constraint that may never be bypassed stays outside the negotiation.
variants.prompt: Recall at candidate depth 200 is short on tail queries. Doubling depth to 400 fixes recall offline but p99 latency passes the target. What is the better next step?
options: Ship depth 400 and add serving copies to absorb the extra work.
Ship depth 400 for head queries only, where traffic and revenue concentrate.
Keep the depth and improve the embeddings or query routing, then re-measure recall.
optionFeedback: Copies raise how many queries run at once; they do not make one deeper query finish faster.
Head queries are the ones already served well, so this spends the budget where recall was not the problem.
Correct: a better retriever can raise recall without the linear fan-out and reranker cost of more candidates.
variants.hint: Ask whether the problem is how many queries you run or how expensive one query became.
variants.explanation: Larger candidate sets buy recall with fan-out and reranking cost, so a stronger retriever or better routing is the cheaper way to move recall when latency is already at its limit.

variants.title: Give the symptom an owner
variants.context: Each part of a search system answers one question, each freshness clock measures one interval, and each symptom has one owning stage. A relevance gain never cancels a permission leak, and a fast response never makes stale inventory correct.
variants.prompt: Match each part of the search path to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Lexical retrieval
pairs.detail: Which documents contain the evidence, including names, identifiers, and quoted phrases.

pairs.label: Semantic retrieval
pairs.detail: Which documents express the intent, traded against exact recall for latency and memory.

pairs.label: Structured constraints
pairs.detail: Which documents are eligible under permissions, tenant, geography, and safety policy.

pairs.label: Ranking and policy
pairs.detail: Which eligible results should lead, once richer query-document features are affordable.

variants.hint: One of these four is a hard filter rather than a relevance signal.
variants.explanation: Each stage answers a different question, which is why a vector score can never stand in for an eligibility decision.

variants.title: Give the symptom an owner
variants.context: Each part of a search system answers one question, each freshness clock measures one interval, and each symptom has one owning stage. A relevance gain never cancels a permission leak, and a fast response never makes stale inventory correct.
variants.prompt: Match each freshness clock to the interval it measures.

pairs.label: Source lag
pairs.detail: Time from an authoritative commit to the change reaching ingestion.

pairs.label: Representation lag
pairs.detail: Time from ingestion until lexical fields and embeddings are ready.

pairs.label: Serving lag
pairs.detail: Time from a complete index generation to every replica using it.

variants.hint: Follow one edit from the database to the user and mark the handoffs.
variants.explanation: Three clocks are tracked separately because a stall in any one of them produces the same user-visible symptom of stale results.

variants.title: Give the symptom an owner
variants.context: Each part of a search system answers one question, each freshness clock measures one interval, and each symptom has one owning stage. A relevance gain never cancels a permission leak, and a fast response never makes stale inventory correct.
variants.prompt: Match each production symptom to the stage that owns it.

pairs.label: A relevant item never appears at any rank
pairs.detail: Inspect recall by retriever, filter selectivity, embedding versions, and candidate depth.

pairs.label: Good candidates are ordered badly
pairs.detail: Replay source ranks and feature values, then compare the fused order with the learned order.

pairs.label: Only tail latency regresses
pairs.detail: Break down child deadlines, queue time, shard fan-out, cold segments, and reranker batches.

pairs.label: Fast results are stale or forbidden
pairs.detail: Inspect source, representation, and serving lag plus generation skew, and stop serving unprovable results.

variants.hint: Ask whether the item was ever in the candidate set before blaming the order.
variants.explanation: Ranking can only reorder what retrieval found, so mapping a symptom to its owning stage is what stops teams from tuning a reranker to fix a missing candidate.
